segments.title: The Fog and What It Hides: Opening the Case

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the great novels in the English language.
Charles Dickens published Bleak House in monthly parts between 1852 and 1853, and it has never really let go of its readers since.
It is a novel of fog and chancery, of orphans and aristocrats, of a legal system so monstrous it has become almost comic — and of extraordinary human warmth persisting in spite of all that.
With me today are three readers who know this novel deeply and differently, and who I suspect will not agree on everything — which is exactly as it should be.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don with a lifelong commitment to reading fiction as moral imagination.
He believes great literature is finally about character tested by circumstance — about goodness, weakness, and what we owe each other — and he brings that lens to Dickens with bracing rigour.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions literature depicts.
He can tell you exactly what the Court of Chancery was, what it cost, and what it destroyed — and he will, because it matters enormously to understanding this book.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She brings the reader's eye — the ear, really — for what is funny, what is moving, and what makes you stop and re-read a sentence out loud to the nearest person.
We begin where the novel itself begins — with atmosphere, with setting, with the first impressions a house makes on those who enter it.
Caroline, Bleak House the house — Esther's first glimpse of it — is one of the great domestic arrivals in fiction.
It really is — and what strikes me every time is how thoroughly it confounds expectation.
We have a house called Bleak House — that name does its work on you before you even arrive.

And then Esther walks in and finds flowers in chintz and paper, oval engravings of haymaking ladies, stiff courtly chairs each attended by — and this is the detail that gets me — a little page of a stool for greater state.
It is comic and tender at exactly the same moment.
And then the passage builds and builds until it arrives at this extraordinary cumulative sentence — let me read it.

"with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House"
That phrase — a low accompaniment to everything we heard — is almost musical notation.
Dickens is telling you how to experience the house — as a chord, not a catalogue.
Caroline is right to fix on that sentence — it performs what it describes.
The wind sounding a low accompaniment: Dickens folds the natural world into the domestic one without effort, without strain.
But I want to draw attention to the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw.
The house as Jarndyce — that is the moral point.
Atmosphere, in Dickens, is never merely pictorial — it is the externalisation of a character's inner condition.
Jarndyce's generosity literally illuminates the building — those windows softened by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the starlight night.

The quaint variety of the furnishings — birds staring at trout, portrait brothers separated by rooms — is the signature of an intelligence that delights in the particular, the individual, the unrepeatable.
And that, I would argue, is the novel's deepest conviction: that persons matter more than systems.
I won't quarrel with Edmund on the particulars — the passage is glorious — but I'd set it against a very different kind of house that shadows this novel.
Because before we had Bleak House the refuge, Dickens gives us Chesney Wold — the Dedlock estate, which has its own legend, its own ghost, its own curse.
There is a crippled woman in its past who is told to keep silent about her suffering — and refuses to.
She drops on the terrace pavement, and when her husband comes to lift her, she repulses him and delivers what I can only call a constitutional indictment of an entire class.

"I will die here where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen for my step!"
The gothic machinery is deliberate — but it is also historically precise.
An aristocratic house built on the suppression of inconvenient suffering — that is not only a ghost story, that is a description of the English landed gentry's entire social compact.
She walked until she could not walk — and then she promised to keep walking.
That repetition — I will walk here, I will walk here, I will walk here — is almost incantatory.
Dickens is using the cadences of a curse — biblical, implacable.
And it answers Edmund's point in a way — character does persist, even beyond the grave in this novel.
But it's the character of the wronged, not the powerful, that endures.
I accept that correction with some pleasure, actually.
The ghostly walker of Chesney Wold is a wonderful figure precisely because her defiance is entirely private and entirely inexhaustible.
She never complains of her suffering to any living person — only to the house itself, and only in the future tense.
That, I think, is Dickens showing us that the deepest moral claims are not made in courts — not even courts of conscience.
There is a third kind of house in this opening movement of the novel — and it is the most fragile.
The household that Jarndyce assembles around him — Esther, Richard, Ada — is not built on inheritance or on stone.
It is built on confidence — his word — and on the possibility of love.
When Jarndyce addresses Richard and Ada about the possibility he had long contemplated, he is extraordinarily careful with his language.

"When I contemplated these relations between us four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together."
Afar off — he uses it twice in that speech.
It is a man trying very hard not to press what he has imagined upon those he loves — and succeeding, just barely.
Don't be shy, Ada, don't be shy — that parenthesis is so alive on the page.
It breaks the formal rhythm of the sentence entirely — you can hear him actually speaking, actually blushing a little on her behalf.
And the tenderness of it is exactly the thing that makes the novel's later tragedy so painful — because this is what is at stake.
This warmth, this brightness — and how precarious it all is.
Three houses, then — and three quite different relationships to the past, to obligation, and to hope.
That tension between the warmth Dickens generates and the forces that threaten it — legal, institutional, ghostly — is going to run through everything we discuss today.
Coming up: the fog itself — and the machinery of the Court of Chancery that Dickens saw as the great engine of English misery.

segments.title: Richard's Long Decline: Ambition to Ruin

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see what it's really made of.
Today's deep dive concerns one of the novel's most heartbreaking arcs: the slow, self-willed destruction of Richard Carstone.
But to understand what Richard loses, we first have to understand what he was given — and by whom.
With me today are three guests who bring very different eyes to this story.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don and critic of the old school, who reads novels as moral dramas about character tested by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who will anchor us in the institutional realities Dickens is mapping.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and passionate re-reader, who cares above all about the experience of the prose on the page.
Let's begin where Dickens begins Richard's story — with hope, and with a warning.
What strikes me every time I return to these early chapters is how much Dickens invests in making Richard genuinely loveable.
He's warm, enthusiastic, open-hearted — and so is Ada, of course — and together they're almost unbearably bright.
Esther describes the scene where they confide in her, one on either side, with such affection.
She writes: "They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That parenthesis — "I enjoyed it too much myself" — is one of those small Dickensian gifts that makes you love Esther completely.
But Esther is also the one who introduces the sober counter-note, the recognition that this love can only come to happiness through constancy, fortitude, and perseverance.
And from the beginning, we know Richard doesn't really hear that part.
What Dickens is dramatising here is something very specific to Richard's social position.
Richard is a young gentleman of good family but no fortune — dependent, entirely, on the outcome of Jarndyce and Jarndyce.
That case was a real type — Chancery suits that dragged for generations, consuming the very estate they were meant to distribute.
So Mr. Jarndyce's advice to Richard in Chapter Thirteen isn't just benevolent counsel — it's a diagnosis of a structural trap.
He says, and I find this extraordinary in its precision:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
The heathen waggoner — that's the man who prays to Hercules to free his stuck cart rather than putting his own shoulder to the wheel.
Jarndyce sees exactly what Richard is becoming — a man waiting for Fortune to do the work effort should do.
James is quite right that Jarndyce diagnoses the condition — but I'd press a little on the word structural.
What Dickens gives us in Richard is not a victim of circumstance but a failure of will — and that distinction matters enormously.
Jarndyce is magnificently clear about this — listen to what follows that injunction:

"If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
By fits and starts — that is Richard entire, from his first appearance to his last.
The tragedy is not that the system destroys him — it is that he lacks the moral fibre to resist it.
Dickens, as always, is more interested in character than in legislation.
I take Edmund's point about will — but I think Dickens is also doing something more tender than a moral verdict.
There's that passage at the end of Chapter Thirteen — Esther watching Richard and Ada walk away through sunlit rooms.
It's one of the most beautifully weighted passages in the whole novel, and it works entirely through light.

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
And then — the turn:
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
Dickens earns that shadow by making the light so absolutely real first.
That's not a moral verdict — it's a lament.
Caroline's reading of that passage is exactly right — and it helps explain why readers who never think about Chancery still weep over Richard.
But I want to draw attention to something else in Chapter Thirteen — the remarkable grace Jarndyce shows in leaving the door open.
He says to them — and this is genuinely unusual for a Victorian guardian:
"Don't be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be nothing monstrous or uncommon in it."
He has already anticipated that they may change — and he refuses to make shame the instrument of control.
For a man who could so easily have wielded power, that restraint is remarkable.
And Richard, of course, will eventually make it impossible to honour.
I want to bring in a figure who stands at the opposite end of this moral spectrum — Mr. Tulkinghorn.
Because Dickens, I think, is not only tracing Richard's decline — he is meditating throughout this novel on what it means to be utterly unreadable.
Tulkinghorn, in Chapter Eleven, is described with one of the most devastating similes in the novel.
"As easily might the tone of a delicate musical instrument be inferred from its case, as the tone of Mr. Tulkinghorn from his case."
The man has shown nothing but his shell — patience, impatience, attention, abstraction — none of it can be read.
Richard is destroyed partly because he cannot conceal anything — his soul is entirely on his face.
Tulkinghorn is destroyed partly because he conceals everything — and concealment in this novel is a form of corruption.
Dickens is running both trajectories simultaneously, and the contrast is mordant.
That contrast between Tulkinghorn and Richard is one I hadn't articulated quite so cleanly — Edmund, that's very fine.
What it makes me think about is the word Esther keeps returning to around Richard — hope.
Richard's openness, his transparency, is the same quality as his hope — and both become his undoing.
He hopes so entirely in the case — so fits and starts of hope — that constancy in the ordinary business of living becomes impossible.
And Esther watches this, narrates it, loves him all the same — and that is what makes it unbearable.
I should like to close by returning to a passage that has perhaps the least obvious bearing on Richard — and yet, I think, the most profound.
In Chapter Fifty-Eight, Dickens reflects on Sir Leicester's fidelity to Lady Dedlock — his conquest of his own pride for her sake.
And the narrator reaches what I consider one of the most quietly magnificent sentences in the book:
"In such a light both aspire alike, both rise alike, both children of the dust shine equally."
Children of the dust — that is what all these characters are, from Sir Leicester to Richard to Tulkinghorn.
What separates them is not rank or intelligence or opportunity — but what they choose to do with their dust.
Richard chooses — however pitiably — to let Chancery do the choosing for him.
Children of the dust shine equally — what a note to pause on.

We've moved today from the warmth of that early hope between Richard and Ada, through Jarndyce's extraordinary counsel, to the gothic blankness of Tulkinghorn — and back again to the question of what any of us do with our circumstances.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for bringing such different and illuminating lights to these passages.
Next time, we turn to the fog — literal and institutional — that Dickens builds at the very opening of the novel, and what it does to everyone who breathes it.
Until then — keep reading.

segments.title: The Weight of Secrets: Lady Dedlock's Unraveling

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme where we slow down and look closely at one of the great novels in the English language.
Today we're deep in the architecture of secrecy — specifically, the slow, cold chess match between Lady Dedlock and the lawyer Tulkinghorn.
With me are three readers who bring very different lenses to this extraordinary material.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and literary critic who reads Dickens above all as a moralist — a writer of character under pressure.
Professor James Blackstone brings the historian's eye — he knows what these institutions actually were, and what they meant for the people caught inside them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who cares passionately about what the prose sounds like, and which characters deserve better.
Let's begin with Tulkinghorn himself — the man who arrives, always at the same measured pace, always wearing what Dickens calls his expressionless mask.
Tulkinghorn is, I think, one of Dickens's supreme achievements in characterisation — and the more alarming for being so understated.
He arrives at Chesney Wold in a sentence that is itself almost ceremonial in its measured pace.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb. Every crease. The man is not merely a keeper of secrets — he is constituted by them.
And then Dickens asks the question that I find genuinely haunting: whether his soul is devoted to the great, or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells.
We are never told. That unresolved ambiguity is the source of all his power.
What arrests me every time is that final clause — "he is his own client in that matter, and will never betray himself."
It turns the legal metaphor back on the lawyer with this exquisite precision.
He treats his own inner life as a brief he is retained to protect. There's something almost admirable in it, and something deeply sinister.
And what Dickens does so brilliantly in these chapters is stage the encounter between Tulkinghorn's kind of secrecy and Lady Dedlock's kind.
Hers is desperate, existential. His is professional, almost serene.
There's a legal reality underpinning all of this that makes Tulkinghorn's position even more formidable than Edmund suggests.

A family solicitor of this period had access that went far beyond what we would consider professional today — he was a repository of title deeds, wills, private letters, and family history going back generations.
He had, effectively, the power to destroy a family simply by choosing when to speak and when to remain silent.
And that is precisely what Dickens is dramatising when he shows us the message Sir Leicester reads aloud, so awkwardly, to Lady Dedlock.
The message that reads, in Tulkinghorn's careful legal diction:
"I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him."
Those four final words. Separated. Absolute. It is a declaration, and it is a threat.
And yet the medium of delivery is Sir Leicester — oblivious, stately, fumbling with his eyeglass.
Dickens gives us this devastating intelligence passed through the most benign of conduits, entirely unaware of what he carries.
It is, in structural terms, very fine comedy placed in the service of very dark material.
And Lady Dedlock's response — merely looking a little irritated at the delay with the eyeglass — is one of the great acts of controlled performance in Victorian fiction.
That detail about looking irritated at the eyeglass — it's almost unbearably good, isn't it.
Because from outside it reads as aristocratic impatience — perfectly in character for Lady Dedlock.
But we know what is actually happening inside her. The irritation is the only safe emotion available.
Then Dickens gives us the scene's real portrait, and I want to read it in full because I think it is magnificent.
"During the utterance of every word of this short dialogue, Lady Dedlock and Mr. Tulkinghorn, without any other alteration in their customary deportment, have looked very steadily at one another."

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
"All this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts." That phrase — for the time — is the most quietly terrifying thing in the chapter.
The repetition of evermore is doing something structurally very important there.
It converts what might have been a single dramatic moment into a condition — something ongoing, permanent, inescapable.
And Dickens confirms this when he moves forward in time and shows us their subsequent meetings at Chesney Wold.
The passage describes them meeting again at dinner — again, next day — again, for many days in succession.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
The phrase exhausted deity is quietly devastating — it captures both her social elevation and her profound inner depletion.
She is performing grandeur while being slowly destroyed by what she knows and what she fears.
And Tulkinghorn's counterpart description is equally precise — the speechless repository of noble confidences, so oddly out of place and yet so perfectly at home.
Oddly out of place and yet perfectly at home. The paradox is exact.
He belongs neither to the aristocratic world he serves nor to any other — he exists in the interstices of society, as power so often does.
Burke observed that the cold neutrality of an impartial judge is not benevolence. Tulkinghorn is something darker still — he is impartiality in the service of an undisclosed agenda.
There's another dimension to Lady Dedlock's secret that we haven't yet touched on — its reach into the next generation.
Because hidden alongside the Chesney Wold performances is the fact that Lady Dedlock has a child she has never acknowledged — and the child, Esther, eventually learns what little she can.
Caroline, you've wanted to speak about the passage in which Mr. Jarndyce explains to Esther the terms of her guardian's original instructions.
Yes — because this passage shows us the other side of Lady Dedlock's secret, and it is heartbreaking in a very quiet way.
Jarndyce is telling Esther what he knows of the woman who arranged for her to be educated and cared for — but who refused to be named.
He tells her, in this careful, legal-sounding phrasing:

"That she was, if there were any ties of blood in such a case, the child's aunt. That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
For any human consideration. There is something almost inhuman in that resolution — and yet we understand it completely.
Lady Dedlock is preserving Esther the only way she knows how — by denying her.
And then Jarndyce says those four plain words — my dear, I have told you all — and the smallness of the information is itself a wound.
The language of the message is worth noticing — "assumed name," "ties of blood in such a case" — it is the language of legal instruments.
Lady Dedlock — or whoever she was then — has translated her most intimate relationship into a transaction.
And the intermediary is, significantly, Mr. Kenge — another lawyer, another repository of dangerous knowledge.
What strikes me as a historian is how completely the institutions of the period — Chancery, the family solicitor, the confidential agent — enable and sustain this secrecy.
They are not incidental to Lady Dedlock's tragedy. They are its scaffolding.
I'd want to add that the steadfastness of Lady Dedlock's resolution — that phrase James just quoted — is presented without irony.
Dickens has no contempt for her. He renders her resolution as genuinely formidable — perhaps the most formidable thing about her.
The tragedy is not that she is weak, but that she is strong in precisely the wrong direction — strength deployed in the service of concealment rather than connection.
That, to my mind, is where the novel's moral imagination is at its deepest.
Strength in the wrong direction — that's a phrase worth sitting with.

We've seen today how Dickens constructs this entire web of secrecy — through Tulkinghorn's impenetrable professional mask, through Lady Dedlock's exquisite social performance, and through the institutions that make concealment not just possible but structurally necessary.
In our next segment, we'll follow the consequences — what happens when the threads of that web begin, one by one, to pull loose.

segments.title: A Crossing Sweeper's Lot: Jo and the Society That Abandons Him

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series working through Dickens's great novel chapter by chapter, passage by passage.
Today we're in the early chapters — the courts, the slums, and the figures who fall through every crack society offers.
With me are three voices I rely on to make this novel speak properly.
Sir Edmund Leigh, retired Oxford don, who believes the novel's genius lives in moral imagination — in individual character tested by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone, legal and social historian, who knows exactly what these institutions were, what they cost, and who paid.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel since her teens, who cares above all about the experience of the prose on the page and in the ear.
This segment centres on Jo — the crossing sweeper — and on the dead man the world called Nemo.
James, I want to start with you, because before Jo can testify, we first have to reckon with the room where Nemo dies.
That room is one of the most methodically composed pieces of social pathology in the novel.
Dickens doesn't spare you the inventory — the patchwork, the lean-ribbed ticking, the coarse sacking.
These are not atmospheric flourishes.
They are the actual furnishings of extreme poverty in mid-Victorian London — what you slept on when there was nothing else.
But what arrests me is the moment the narrator shifts from what Tulkinghorn sees to what he tastes.
"through the general sickliness and faintness, and the odour of stale tobacco, there comes into the lawyer's mouth the bitter, vapid taste of opium."
The lawyer doesn't merely observe this death — he physically ingests it.
It enters him.
That is a remarkable observation, James, and I think it points to something Dickens understood with extraordinary precision.
Tulkinghorn is not a man of feeling — he is a man of papers, of secrets held like property.
And yet his body registers what his moral imagination refuses to.
The prose enacts a moral fact through a physiological sensation — that is the mark of a writer at full command.
And then of course there is what follows Nemo's death — the inquest, the witnesses, the coroner's court.
Dickens gives us that extraordinary passage about the dead man's anonymity.
"lies there with no more track behind him that any one can trace than a deserted infant."
Forty-five years of life — and nothing recoverable.
That is not a social thesis — it is a human tragedy, complete in one sentence.
The image that won't leave me is the coffin standing by the old portmanteau.
That word portmanteau — it implies travel, a life going somewhere.
And Dickens puts it right beside the coffin, and lets them share the room all night.
That's not a paragraph — that's a poem.
And it prepares you for Jo — because Jo is the one person in that courtroom who actually knew this man.
Before Jo speaks, we get Mrs. Piper — and she is something else entirely.
There's this magnificent moment where she describes the dead man — she insists on calling him 'the plaintive' — and the narrator tells us quite deadpan that she was reported to have sold himself.
"the plaintive—so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased—was reported to have sold himself."
She's comic, she's infuriating, she's completely recognisable — the neighbourhood expert who knows everything and understands nothing.
Mrs. Piper is also doing something legally specific — she's offering character evidence at a coroner's inquest.
And it's worth noting she's taken seriously, while Jo is not.
What Dickens gives us in Jo's testimony is the stark arithmetic of exclusion.
"No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school."
Six words — and then six more.
Each category of human connection — family, friendship, education — struck off in a single noun.
Jo is then deemed an incompetent witness because he cannot swear a meaningful oath — he doesn't know enough to understand what an oath is.
The law that failed to educate him now excludes him for his ignorance.
That is precisely where I'd want to pause, James, because it's a powerful point — but I think Dickens is making an even larger claim.
Jo does know two things — what a broom is for, and that it's wicked to tell a lie.
He doesn't know who taught him either.
That is not merely social commentary — it is a theological proposition.
Moral knowledge exists in this child independently of every institution that has abandoned him.
Burke might call it natural law.
Dickens simply calls it Jo.
And then we get the passage where Dickens addresses Jo directly — narrator to character — which is one of the strangest and most moving things in the book.
"Jo, is it thou?" — that sudden intimacy, that biblical register — it stops the novel cold.
And then the thing he says — this child who has been found legally incompetent to speak — that becomes his salvation.
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
The misspelling matters — Dickens prints the dialect exactly, and it becomes grace.
The law has said his words count for nothing.
Dickens says — no, these four words are a ray of light.
What I keep returning to is the passage about Nemo and Jo before the inquest — the moment of human recognition between them.
Dickens is quite specific about the mechanism of compassion here.
The man turned to look at Jo shivering in a doorway — and the turning back is everything.
He found that the boy had not a friend in the world.
"Neither have I. Not one!" and gave him the price of a supper and a night's lodging."
These are two people for whom society has no name, no use, no record.
And between them they construct the only community available — mutual recognition and a shared meal.
I find that moment extraordinarily crafted — the rhetorical parity of their destitution.
Nemo doesn't pity the boy from above — he recognises himself.
That is the novel's deepest moral argument, I think — that the capacity for goodness is distributed without regard for rank or education.
And the novel makes this claim not through a speech or a sermon — but through a cold night, a doorway, and a supper.
That is a powerful place to take a breath.
Jo's testimony — excluded, dismissed — and yet that one sentence carries more moral weight than anything offered by the court.
In the next segment, we move from the inquest outward — to the institutions that produce and perpetuate this world.
Do stay with us.

segments.title: Dickens at Play: Humor in the Darkness

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the great Victorian novels apart sentence by sentence to see what makes it tick.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring something that often gets lost when people talk about this novel's darkness and indignation — its extraordinary comic genius.
Joining me today are three voices who know this novel with uncommon intimacy.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and traditionalist critic who reads Dickens above all as a great moral storyteller — and who will keep us honest about what the comedy is actually doing to character.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows what Chancery actually was — the machinery behind the satire — and can tell us why Dickens's jokes are sharper than they look.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and close reader who has lived with this novel since her teens and has a gift for catching the verbal music on the page.
Caroline, let's begin with you — because the novel opens not with a character or a plot, but with weather, and it's weather of a very peculiar kind.
What strikes me every time I open this novel is that the first chapter is essentially a joke — a sustained, deadpan, absolutely magnificent joke.
Dickens opens with a world so mired in mud and fog and soot that ordinary language won't quite cover it — so he reaches for the prehistoric.
The sentence I return to again and again — it's almost the first full sentence of the entire novel — begins with the mud.

"As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A Megalosaurus — waddling — up Holborn Hill.
The comedy comes from the absolute confidence of the absurdity — Dickens doesn't say "one might imagine a dinosaur," he says it would not be wonderful to meet one.
And then the bathos of "waddling" — that single verb does so much work.
I think Caroline is exactly right to fasten on that verb.
"Waddling" is not a word that dignifies — it's a word that slightly humiliates — and Dickens deploys it against the modern city, not against the creature.
But I would resist the reading that this is pure comedy, or comedy for its own sake.
The comedy here is doing something that Johnson would have recognised — it uses laughter to strip away false dignity and reveal the thing as it truly is.
The city in November, mired in primordial mud, is a city that has not progressed — it has merely accumulated, at what Dickens rather brilliantly calls compound interest.
The joke and the moral indictment are the same thing.
Edmund makes a point I find genuinely compelling — the compound interest image is remarkable precisely because it's economic language applied to filth.
In 1852, when Bleak House began appearing in serial parts, the mud of London streets was a genuine public-health catastrophe — it was, among other things, the vector for cholera.
And Dickens, throughout this novel, keeps making the same satirical move: taking the bureaucratic language of profit and business and applying it to decay and death.
Which brings me to a passage from much later in the novel that reads almost as a statement of method.
"The one great principle of the English law is to make business for itself."
Five words — "to make business for itself" — and suddenly every absurdity in the novel clicks into place as not absurdity at all, but as rational behaviour by an irrational system.
The comedy is the system's self-portrait, painted without shame.
And the cheek of that final clause — "and surely they will cease to grumble" — is something I find almost physically funny.
Dickens is pretending to be perfectly reasonable, offering the public an explanation that ought to satisfy them — but the explanation is monstrous.
It's the same comedy he performs with Lady Dedlock — and that passage is one of my favourites in the whole novel.
Lady Dedlock believes herself to be utterly inscrutable — sees herself in her glass and is entirely satisfied with the mystery she presents.
But Dickens tells us that every dim little star revolving about her — from her maid upward — has her perfectly mapped.
"Who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
That image is wickedly exact — the aristocracy as a toy fleet, captured without their knowing it.
The Gulliver allusion is rather fine — and it works, I think, because Swift is always in the background when Dickens reaches for his sharpest satirical instruments.
But what Dickens adds — and this is characteristically his — is the warmth of specific observation.
Mr. Sladdery the librarian, saying — with perfect sincerity — "I can turn them round my finger," and Dickens noting that in this he does not exaggerate at all.
The phrase "honest man" applied to a man confessing his manipulation of the aristocracy — that is the joke.
And the joke's staying power comes from the fact that it is also, entirely and precisely, the truth.
What I find interesting about these comic passages is that they're all, in some sense, about the comedy of surveillance — about who is actually watching whom.
Lady Dedlock thinks she is being deferred to, when she is being managed.
And poor Mr. Snagsby — who is being watched by his wife, in a passage that is simultaneously farcical and genuinely unsettling.
The language Dickens uses there escalates from domestic comedy into something almost biblical.

"And into whatsoever atmosphere of secrecy his own shadow may pass, let all concerned in the secrecy beware! For the watchful Mrs. Snagsby is there too — bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
"Bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh" — that's the marriage formula from Genesis, turned here into a sentence of inescapable domestic surveillance.
It is very funny — and it is also, if you are Mr. Snagsby, absolutely terrifying.
"Shadow of his shadow" — that triple repetition is so good, and Dickens earns it because he's built up to it with "bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh."
And then there's the Smallweed passage — which is comedy of a different, grimier kind.
Mr. Bucket whispers his account of the Smallweed family's internal warfare over a document — and the whisper is everything.
"First the avaricious grandchildren split upon him on account of their objections to his living so unreasonably long, and then they split on one another."
"Living so unreasonably long" — there is no kinder phrase in the English language for that sentiment, and Bucket delivers it without a flicker of irony.
And the old lady who is only outside the conspiracy because she is, as Bucket puts it, "too weak in her mind to drive a bargain" — that is a punchline of genuine blackness.

What unites all of these passages, it seems to me, is that the comedy is always comedy of self-deception — of people who cannot see themselves as others see them, or see themselves only too clearly and don't care.
Lady Dedlock imagines herself inscrutable; the law imagines itself coherent; the Smallweeds imagine themselves shrewd operators.
In each case, the narrative voice cuts through the pretension with perfect courtesy — and it is that courtesy, that surface restraint, which makes the cut so clean.
Burke observed that manners are the foundation of civilisation — Dickens understood that impeccable manners are also the most devastating weapon of the satirist.
Satire with perfect manners — that's a wonderful phrase to carry with us.

What I think we've been circling is something central to how Bleak House works: that its darkness and its comedy are not in tension — they are the same thing, expressed in two registers simultaneously.
The Megalosaurus waddling up Holborn Hill, the shadow of his shadow, the old lady too weak to drive a bargain — all of these make you laugh, and then make you think, and then make you uneasy.
That three-beat movement is, I think, the Dickens signature — and we'll keep listening for it as we move through the novel.

segments.title: The Law's Labyrinth: Property, Inheritance, and Human Cost

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's great novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into the novel's heart: the law, property, inheritance, and the human wreckage they leave behind.
With me are three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing a very different lens.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that the novel's greatness lies in its moral imagination — in what it shows us about character tested by circumstance.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what Chancery was, what it cost, and who paid the price.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and passionate re-reader who knows this novel almost by heart — and who will tell us what makes you stop mid-page and simply stare at a sentence.
Let's begin with the law itself — not as abstraction, but as lived experience, comic and tragic by turns.
The institution Dickens is attacking in Bleak House — the Court of Chancery — was not a fiction or an exaggeration.
It was a court that had grown so procedurally encrusted over centuries that cases routinely outlived the parties who brought them.
And crucially, the people who profited from that delay had every incentive to prevent reform.
Dickens captures this with surgical precision in the figure of Mr. Vholes and in the voice of Mr. Kenge defending him.
Kenge says, with magnificent brazenness: "Repeal it, my dear sir? Never, with my consent."
And then, the killer argument — the one that ends all argument:
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
That is the whole logic of institutional self-preservation, compressed into one sentence.
James is right that Dickens knows this world from the inside — he worked as a law clerk, after all.
But what interests me is the satirical mode Dickens deploys — the mock-parliamentary inquiry, those numbered questions running to half a million.
Question five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine.
The absurdity of that number is itself an argument — a Swiftian argument — about bureaucratic infinity.
And then, the answer that "proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years" — simply: Vholes is a most respectable man.
Respectability — that great Victorian shield — defeats justice simply by being invoked.
What strikes me every time I re-read that passage is its extraordinary comic tempo — the questions accelerating, the answers retreating.
Delay? Yes, some delay. Great expense? Most assuredly they cannot be gone through for nothing.
Each answer is technically truthful and utterly evasive — like watching a man sidestep every question while walking calmly forward.
And then the wonderful barefaced pivot — unspeakable vexation, asks the committee.
"I am not prepared to say that. They have never given ME any vexation; quite the contrary."
That capital ME on the page — you can hear the outrage Dickens felt when he wrote it.
And yet the law's machinery doesn't only grind in cold institutions — it spills out into the countryside, into personal feuds, into something almost farcical.
Boythorn's battle with Sir Leicester Dedlock over a right of way is one of the great comic set-pieces in the novel — and it says something rather precise about law as a vehicle for class war.
Boythorn is one of my absolute favourite characters in the novel — this magnificent volcano of a man.
He erupts in the most beautifully constructed sentences — superlative piled on superlative.
Listen to this — it builds like a legal brief written by a man in a delicious fury:
"the most stiff-necked, arrogant imbecile, pig-headed numskull, ever, by some inexplicable mistake of Nature, born in any station of life but a walking-stick's!"
A walking-stick's! — meaning: fit only to be a walking stick. That throwaway last phrase is a masterpiece.
And then the escalation — the fire engine, the gate chopped down at dawn, the humane man-traps, the split peas.
What makes Boythorn work as a character — and not merely as a comic turn — is that his excess is principled.
He is not simply eccentric. He genuinely believes that Sir Leicester has no right, and he intends to defend that belief personally, physically, and with boundless theatrical invention.
The passage captures this perfectly in its closing rhythm — the tit-for-tat of legal actions rendered as a war chant:
"He brings actions for trespass; I bring actions for trespass. He brings actions for assault and battery; I defend them and continue to assault and batter. Ha, ha, ha!"
The laughter — Ha, ha, ha — is not nervous or ironic. It is the laugh of a man who genuinely enjoys himself.
There is something Burkean in Boythorn — a stubborn defence of what is one's own against arbitrary enclosure by rank.
Edmund's point about enclosure is sharper than it might sound — rights of way were a genuine flashpoint in the Victorian period.
The enclosure of common land and footpaths by landowners like Sir Leicester was an ongoing social injury.
And notice how Dickens gives Boythorn a language that mirrors Sir Leicester's — formal letters, counter-letters, legal precision — but then explodes it with fire engines.
The comedy is also a kind of argument: the man without the baronetcy can only win by being more outrageous than the system itself.
But behind the comedy — and sometimes within it — there is a much darker current in this novel about what law and pride cost people in intimate, private lives.
James, you've been thinking about the passage in which Jarndyce tells Esther the story of Boythorn and Lady Dedlock's sister — a story about sacrifice, pride, and a kind of self-inflicted death.
It's one of the passages that stops you cold in the middle of a chapter full of legal machinery.
Because here the real cost isn't financial — it's a human life voluntarily extinguished out of a combined sense of wounded honour and protective love.
Jarndyce speaks of how she wrote to Boythorn, and Dickens gives us the exact content of that letter in reported speech:
"she wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did."
Died to him — as in literal truth she did. Dickens repeats that phrase, and it lands like a weight.
And then the reasoning — that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too.
She is not sacrificing herself despite understanding him — she is sacrificing herself because she understands him completely.
This is precisely where I find Dickens at his most morally serious — and most moving.
The phrase that haunts me is this one: she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it.
"she made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it. She did both, I fear."
She did both, I fear. Four words — I fear — and Jarndyce's entire grief is in them.
No sentimentality. No elaboration. Just the fact, and the fear that it is true.
And it reframes Boythorn entirely — the man you've just been laughing at for twenty pages is suddenly a figure of tremendous, quiet pathos.
He never saw her again. Never heard of her from that hour. Nor did anyone.
That last clause — nor did any one — is placed with such deliberate quietness that it almost disappears, and yet it's devastating.
It erases her from the world entirely — no trace, no witness, no record.
Pride — and its costs — runs through all of these passages, doesn't it.
And nowhere is it more urgent than in Mrs. Rouncewell's plea to Lady Dedlock in chapter fifty-five.
Mrs. Rouncewell is a character who earns everything she says through her sheer dignity and consistency across the novel.
She has served the Dedlock family her entire life — and her plea to Lady Dedlock is not servile, it is direct.
She says, in a frightened whisper — and Dickens tells us it is a frightened whisper — but then she speaks at length:

"My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves."
That repetition — pray, oh, pray — is not rhetorical ornamentation. It is the sound of a mother begging.
And the social analysis embedded in it is precise: she knows Lady Dedlock has the power, and she knows that Lady Dedlock's pride is what stands between her son and justice.
What moves me is the self-awareness in her speech — she knows exactly how the distance between them looks from Lady Dedlock's vantage point.
She says: you are not familiar with your friends; and all who admire you — and all do — know you to be one far away from themselves who can't be approached close.
That parenthetical — and all do — is so shrewd. It's not flattery. It's a mirror held up.
And then, at the close, she says something that breaks the heart in its simplicity:
"I am so humble in my place and you are by nature so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child."
She doesn't demand understanding. She concedes its absence. And still she asks.
And Dickens certifies her sincerity with his own authorial voice — the old housekeeper pleads with genuine simplicity.
In a novel full of characters performing feeling, that word genuine carries enormous weight.
The contrast with Lady Dedlock's habitual distance is not social criticism so much as it is moral portraiture.
One woman has chosen armour. The other has none. And Dickens leaves no doubt which he values more.
Let's close this segment with a passage that takes all of this — the law, the secrets, the disappearances — and renders it as atmosphere.
Edmund, you've been holding chapter fifty-eight — George patrolling the empty rooms of Chesney Wold.
It's a passage that rewards slow reading, because Dickens is doing something formally very precise here.
George moves through the house with a light held at arm's length — and the narrative enumerates what he is thinking of: his boyhood, the murdered man, the missing lady, the master upstairs.
All the novel's principal griefs gathered in a single consciousness, moving through a single house.
And then Dickens gives us the central image of the whole passage:
"he MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy."
"But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
Blank — repeated — is the great word of this passage. Not sinister. Not threatening. Simply empty.
The horror is that there is no horror — only absence, where something should be.
And the MIGHT — capitalised, just as the ME was capitalised in Vholes's evidence — is doing extraordinary work.
He might see something. He doesn't. But the fact that he might is already a form of haunting.
Chesney Wold throughout the novel has been a place of oppressive grandeur — all that Ghost's Walk, those portraits.
And now it is simply blank. The curse, if there was one, has consumed itself.
There's a historical irony in this image too — the great house patrolled not by its lord but by the trooper son of its housekeeper.
George carries his own complicated relationship to the institution of Chesney Wold — childhood there, years away, now returned as a kind of caretaker.
The house that once organised his entire world — the great house, the baronet, the proper order of things — is now dependent on him for its light.
Blank as the darkness above and below — and blank too, perhaps, as the promise that the law would one day deliver justice to the people it was meant to serve.
That image — the solitary trooper with a lamp, moving through empty grandeur — feels like the novel's own verdict on everything we've been discussing.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the novel's other great preoccupation — the question of identity, and what it costs to conceal who you are.

segments.title: Entanglement and Redemption: Where the Threads Bind

utterances.text: We've spent this episode tracing the currents that run through Bleak House — the law, the fog, the hidden connections between lives.
In this final segment, we want to pull the threads together — to ask what the novel ultimately makes of entanglement, of redemption, and of the cost of both.
Edmund, James, Caroline — you've each, in different ways, been circling these questions all episode.
Edmund, I'd like to begin with you — and with a passage that I think is one of the most extraordinary pieces of direct speech in the entire novel.
Yes — and it is a passage that tends to silence the clever reader, which is itself a considerable achievement.
The brickmaker, on the floor of that terrible room, does something quite remarkable: he seizes the moral initiative from the charitable visitor.
He knows exactly what Mrs. Pardiggle has come to do, and he performs her questions before she can ask them.
The effect is devastating — not because he is sympathetic, but because he is accurate.
He says, in effect:
"Is my daughter a-washin? Yes, she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That's wot we drinks.
How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead!

An't my place dirty? Yes, it is dirty—it's nat'rally dirty, and it's nat'rally onwholesome; and we've had five dirty and onwholesome children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them, and for us besides."
That final clause — "so much the better for them" — is the kind of thing that a comfortable reader wants to flinch from.
But it is also, on its own terms, a perfectly coherent moral position.
The novel does not let us dismiss him.
Edmund is right that the brickmaker is accurate — and historically, almost forensically accurate.
The water described in that passage was a genuine public health catastrophe in the 1850s — the kind that killed thousands before Bazalgette's sewers changed everything.
What's striking is that the man itemises his own degradation with a kind of grim pride.
He has been surveyed, questioned, and catalogued so many times by the philanthropic machinery of the age that he can run the procedure himself.
And that, to my mind, is Dickens's real charge against institutional charity — not that it is useless, but that it turns human beings into specimens.
What gets me every time is the rhythm of it.
That repeated structure — the question, then the answer, then the unbearable elaboration.
He's doing a catechism.
The respectable classes had their catechisms — the church, the Sunday school, the charitable tract.
And he has learnt theirs well enough to invert it entirely, making it serve his fury rather than their condescension.
But then Dickens does something even more devastating later in the same chapter.
After the rage, there is a moment of almost unbearable tenderness — Esther's handkerchief laid over a dead infant.
And then Esther, looking back, reflects on how little she understood what she was doing in that moment.
"How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the child through Ada's drooping hair as her pity bent her head—
how little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast!"
That is the novel's great structural secret: the objects, the gestures, the small acts of compassion — they travel.
Caroline has identified what I regard as the moral architecture of the novel.
It is not a novel of grand resolutions.
It is a novel of small acts whose consequences ripple far beyond what any character can foresee.
Esther wraps a dead child in her handkerchief — a handkerchief that will later find its way to a woman whose life is one long concealed catastrophe.
The halo Esther imagines around the child is not sentimentality — it is Providence rendered in prose.
Though I confess the novel is considerably less sanguine about Providence when it comes to Richard Carstone.
Richard is the novel's other great trajectory — and one that the novel treats with a kind of sorrowful rigour.
The contrast drawn between Richard and Allan Woodcourt is already visible early on.
Mrs. Badger puts it plainly — and there's a sharpness to her plainness that I find quite wonderful.

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
Woodcourt earns his vocation.
Richard merely inherits expectations — and they corrode him.
That, to my mind, is not merely a moral fable — it is a historically precise account of what inherited expectations did to a certain class of young men in Victorian England.
And then, decades of slow ruin later, you get Vholes.
Who is, in his way, one of the most perfectly constructed villains in all of Dickens — because he doesn't feel like a villain at all.
He feels like a system.
The way he wraps his coldest pronouncements in the language of professional duty is almost admirable in its consistency.
He tells Esther, with his diary open to prove his honesty:
"I HAVE carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over to any connexion of Mr. C.'s on any account.
I regard it in the light of a professional duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one."
"Though it can be charged to no one" — there it is.
Vholes performs virtue precisely because virtue is what the system requires him to perform.
Richard never stood a chance against that.
Caroline is right — and I say this as someone who is generally suspicious of systemic readings.
Vholes is one of the few instances where Dickens creates a character who is, by every visible measure, behaving correctly — and yet the reader knows something monstrous is occurring.
He is, if you like, the moral fog made flesh — procedure without conscience, diligence without soul.
And set against him, poor Richard — who had charm, feeling, and no anchor whatsoever.
What strikes me, pulling all of this together, is how different the novel's two trajectories of ruin actually are.
The brickmaker is ruined by a society that gives him undrinkable water and then hands him a tract.
Richard is ruined by an expectation — by Jarndyce and Jarndyce and the terrible possibility that one day it might be resolved in his favour.
The first ruin is material, systemic, entirely preventable.
The second is psychological, spiritual — and the novel is bleaker about it precisely because there is no one quite to blame.
That distinction feels to me like the heart of what this novel is doing — and what makes it inexhaustible.
It holds the systemic and the individual in the same gaze, without collapsing one into the other.
The handkerchief travels, the fog thickens, Vholes writes in his diary, and the brickmaker drinks his gin.
And Esther goes on — recording, reflecting, surviving, connecting.
My warmest thanks to Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt — three guides I would trust through any fog, Chancery-made or otherwise.
And thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

c6:p46.text:
The furniture, old-fashioned rather than old, like the house, was as
pleasantly irregular. Ada’s sleeping-room was all flowers—in chintz
and paper, in velvet, in needlework, in the brocade of two stiff
courtly chairs which stood, each attended by a little page of a stool
for greater state, on either side of the fire-place. Our sitting-room
was green and had framed and glazed upon the walls numbers of
surprising and surprised birds, staring out of pictures at a real
trout in a case, as brown and shining as if it had been served with
gravy; at the death of Captain Cook; and at the whole process of
preparing tea in China, as depicted by Chinese artists. In my room
there were oval engravings of the months—ladies haymaking in short
waists and large hats tied under the chin, for June; smooth-legged
noblemen pointing with cocked-hats to village steeples, for October.
Half-length portraits in crayons abounded all through the house, but
were so dispersed that I found the brother of a youthful officer of
mine in the china-closet and the grey old age of my pretty young
bride, with a flower in her bodice, in the breakfast-room. As
substitutes, I had four angels, of Queen Anne’s reign, taking a
complacent gentleman to heaven, in festoons, with some difficulty;
and a composition in needlework representing fruit, a kettle, and an
alphabet. All the movables, from the wardrobes to the chairs and
tables, hangings, glasses, even to the pincushions and scent-bottles
on the dressing-tables, displayed the same quaint variety. They
agreed in nothing but their perfect neatness, their display of the
whitest linen, and their storing-up, wheresoever the existence of a
drawer, small or large, rendered it possible, of quantities of
rose-leaves and sweet lavender. Such, with its illuminated windows,
softened here and there by shadows of curtains, shining out upon the
starlight night; with its light, and warmth, and comfort; with its
hospitable jingle, at a distance, of preparations for dinner; with
the face of its generous master brightening everything we saw; and
just wind enough without to sound a low accompaniment to everything
we heard, were our first impressions of Bleak House.

“She had been a lady of a handsome figure and a noble carriage. She
never complained of the change; she never spoke to any one of being
crippled or of being in pain, but day by day she tried to walk upon
the terrace, and with the help of the stone balustrade, went up and
down, up and down, up and down, in sun and shadow, with greater
difficulty every day. At last, one afternoon her husband (to whom she
had never, on any persuasion, opened her lips since that night),
standing at the great south window, saw her drop upon the pavement.
He hastened down to raise her, but she repulsed him as he bent over
her, and looking at him fixedly and coldly, said, ‘I will die here
where I have walked. And I will walk here, though I am in my grave. I
will walk here until the pride of this house is humbled. And when
calamity or when disgrace is coming to it, let the Dedlocks listen
for my step!’”

hope to preserve it. When I contemplated these relations between us
four which have so brightened my life and so invested it with new
interests and pleasures, I certainly did contemplate, afar off, the
possibility of you and your pretty cousin here (don’t be shy, Ada,
don’t be shy, my dear!) being in a mind to go through life together.
I saw, and do see, many reasons to make it desirable. But that was

There he was, of course. They brought a chair on either side of me,
and put me between them, and really seemed to have fallen in love
with me instead of one another, they were so confiding, and so
trustful, and so fond of me. They went on in their own wild way for a
little while—I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself—and
then we gradually fell to considering how young they were, and how
there must be a lapse of several years before this early love could
come to anything, and how it could come to happiness only if it were
real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do
their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and
perseverance, each always for the other’s sake. Well! Richard said
that he would work his fingers to the bone for Ada, and Ada said that
she would work her fingers to the bone for Richard, and they called
me all sorts of endearing and sensible names, and we sat there,
advising and talking, half the night. Finally, before we parted, I
gave them my promise to speak to their cousin John to-morrow.

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”
c13:p118.summary: Mr. Jarndyce advises Richard to trust Providence and his own efforts equally, to combine constancy in love with diligent effort in all pursuits, and never to expect success without genuine commitment.

passed down the adjoining room, on which the sun was shining, and out
at its farther end. Richard with his head bent, and her hand drawn
through his arm, was talking to her very earnestly; and she looked up

“Well!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “That’s rational. Now, hear me, my dears!
I might tell you that you don’t know your own minds yet, that a
thousand things may happen to divert you from one another, that it is
well this chain of flowers you have taken up is very easily broken,
or it might become a chain of lead. But I will not do that. Such
wisdom will come soon enough, I dare say, if it is to come at all. I

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.

“Hush! Hush!” The housekeeper looks round and answers in a frightened
whisper, “My Lady, I have not breathed a word of it, I don’t believe
what’s written in it, I know it can’t be true, I am sure and certain
that it is not true. But my son is in danger, and you must have a
heart to pity me. If you know of anything that is not known to
others, if you have any suspicion, if you have any clue at all, and
any reason for keeping it in your own breast, oh, my dear Lady, think
of me, and conquer that reason, and let it be known! This is the most
I consider possible. I know you are not a hard lady, but you go your
own way always without help, and you are not familiar with your
friends; and all who admire you—and all do—as a beautiful and
elegant lady, know you to be one far away from themselves who can’t
be approached close. My Lady, you may have some proud or angry
reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,
oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been
passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with
genuine simplicity, “I am so humble in my place and you are by nature
so high and distant that you may not think what I feel for my child,
but I feel so much that I have come here to make so bold as to beg
and pray you not to be scornful of us if you can do us any right or
justice at this fearful time!”

c58:p98.text:
The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
c58:p98.summary: George patrols the grand house, his memories of past and present mingling, sensing the shadows of the missing Lady Dedlock and the murdered Tulkinghorn, finding only emptiness.

“Then make it easy for her!” growled the man upon the floor. “I wants
it done, and over. I wants a end of these liberties took with my
place. I wants an end of being drawed like a badger. Now you’re
a-going to poll-pry and question according to custom—I know what
you’re a-going to be up to. Well! You haven’t got no occasion to be
up to it. I’ll save you the trouble. Is my daughter a-washin? Yes,
she IS a-washin. Look at the water. Smell it! That’s wot we drinks.
How do you like it, and what do you think of gin instead! An’t my
place dirty? Yes, it is dirty—it’s nat’rally dirty, and it’s
nat’rally onwholesome; and we’ve had five dirty and onwholesome
children, as is all dead infants, and so much the better for them,
and for us besides. Have I read the little book wot you left? No, I
an’t read the little book wot you left. There an’t nobody here as
knows how to read it; and if there wos, it wouldn’t be suitable to
me. It’s a book fit for a babby, and I’m not a babby. If you was to
leave me a doll, I shouldn’t nuss it. How have I been conducting of
myself? Why, I’ve been drunk for three days; and I’da been drunk four
if I’da had the money. Don’t I never mean for to go to church? No, I
don’t never mean for to go to church. I shouldn’t be expected there,
if I did; the beadle’s too gen-teel for me. And how did my wife get
that black eye? Why, I give it her; and if she says I didn’t, she’s a
Lie!”

c8:p117.text:
How little I thought, when I raised my handkerchief to look upon the
tiny sleeper underneath and seemed to see a halo shine around the
child through Ada’s drooping hair as her pity bent her head—how
little I thought in whose unquiet bosom that handkerchief would come
to lie after covering the motionless and peaceful breast! I only
thought that perhaps the Angel of the child might not be all
unconscious of the woman who replaced it with so compassionate a
hand; not all unconscious of her presently, when we had taken leave,
and left her at the door, by turns looking, and listening in terror
for herself, and saying in her old soothing manner, “Jenny, Jenny!”

“My dear Miss Summerson,” she replied, “on Mr. Carstone’s character
and conduct. He is of such a very easy disposition that probably he
would never think it worth while to mention how he really feels, but
he feels languid about the profession. He has not that positive
interest in it which makes it his vocation. If he has any decided
impression in reference to it, I should say it was that it is a
tiresome pursuit. Now, this is not promising. Young men like Mr.
Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can
do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a
very little money and through years of considerable endurance and
disappointment. But I am quite convinced that this would never be the

c60:p94.text:
“Pardon me,” returned Mr. Vholes, going on in exactly the same inward
and dispassionate manner. “Mr. C. takes certain interests under
certain wills disputed in the suit. It is a term we use. In reference
to Mr. C,’s pursuit of his interests, I mentioned to you, Miss
Summerson, the first time I had the pleasure of seeing you, in my
desire that everything should be openly carried on—I used those
words, for I happened afterwards to note them in my diary, which is
producible at any time—I mentioned to you that Mr. C. had laid down
the principle of watching his own interests, and that when a client
of mine laid down a principle which was not of an immoral (that is to
say, unlawful) nature, it devolved upon me to carry it out. I HAVE
carried it out; I do carry it out. But I will not smooth things over
to any connexion of Mr. C.’s on any account. As open as I was to Mr.
Jarndyce, I am to you. I regard it in the light of a professional
duty to be so, though it can be charged to no one. I openly say,
unpalatable as it may be, that I consider Mr. C.’s affairs in a very
bad way, that I consider Mr. C. himself in a very bad way, and that I
regard this as an exceedingly ill-advised marriage. Am I here, sir?
Yes, I thank you; I am here, Mr. C., and enjoying the pleasure of
some agreeable conversation with Miss Summerson, for which I have to
thank you very much, sir!”
c60:p94.summary: Vholes meticulously documents his conversation in his diary and explains that he must openly declare his belief that Richard's affairs are in very bad way and the marriage was ill-advised, all as professional duty; he then abruptly switches to greeting Richard's arrival.
